task_title: Departure, En Route, and Arrival Operations
objective: By the end of this lesson you can pick and fly the right IFR departure (ODP, SID or diverse), check that your airplane can make the climb gradient, fly airways at legal IFR altitudes with the right reports to ATC, and fly a STAR with its crossing restrictions, using VOR or IFR GPS.
why: Most IFR accidents and pilot deviations happen when the pilot is unsure what the clearance or chart requires: a missed climb gradient, a wrong altitude or a misread clearance. Knowing who protects you from terrain and traffic at each point keeps you safe.

warmup: You are cleared "as filed" from a small airport surrounded by hills, and the tower gives you no departure instructions. After liftoff into the clouds, who is making sure you miss the hills: you, ATC, or the procedure designer?

key_terms.def: A departure built only to clear obstacles. Textual or graphic. You may fly it without an ATC clearance.
An ATC departure route, always graphic. You need an ATC clearance to fly it.
A runway with no ODP: you can turn any direction after reaching 400 ft above the runway end and stay clear of obstacles.
Feet of climb per nautical mile (ft/NM). The standard is 200 ft/NM.
Short clearances to fly a SID or STAR laterally and meet all its published altitude and speed restrictions.
Standard Terminal Arrival: an ATC-coded IFR route from the en route structure into the terminal area.
Minimum En Route Altitude: lowest published altitude between fixes with good nav signals and obstacle clearance.
Minimum Obstruction Clearance Altitude: obstacle clearance for the whole segment, but nav signals only within 22 NM of the VOR.
Minimum Crossing Altitude: the lowest altitude to cross a fix when heading toward a higher MEA.
Minimum Reception Altitude: lowest altitude where you can receive the off-course NAVAID that defines a fix.
The point on an airway where you switch from the VOR behind you to the VOR ahead. Midway unless charted.

chunks.title: Three ways out: ODP, SID or diverse departure

body.p: A departure procedure (DP) gives you obstacle clearance from the runway to the en route structure. There are two kinds: the Obstacle Departure Procedure (ODP) and the Standard Instrument Departure (SID) [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]].

When an airport gets its first instrument approach, a designer checks the departure area. If you can turn any direction from a runway and still miss the obstacles, that runway passes a diverse departure assessment and no ODP is published [[29:32|IPH 1-16]].

head: ODP
SID
rows: Obstacle clearance only, by the least onerous route [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]]
ATC flow, less radio talk, plus obstacle clearance [[29:42|IPH 1-26]]
Text or graphic. Graphic ones have (OBSTACLE) in the title [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]]
No. You may fly it unless ATC assigns a SID or vectors [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]]
Yes. ATC clearance must come first [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]]
TPP Takeoff Minimums and (Obstacle) Departure Procedures section; a "T" on the charts points you there [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9g]]
In the TPP with the airport's procedures [[29:42|IPH 1-26]]

body.p: Diverse and ODP protection only reaches 25 NM (46 NM in mountainous areas). Past that, you are responsible for obstacle clearance if you are not on a published route, are below its MEA or MOCA, or are below an ATC-assigned altitude [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e3]].

callout.text: Part 91 pilots are strongly encouraged to file and fly a DP at night, in marginal VMC and in IMC when one is available [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9c]]. If you fly an ODP that is not in your clearance, tell ATC so they can separate traffic [[29:39|IPH 1-23]].

ATC will only assign an ODP from a nontowered airport when it is needed for separation from other aircraft [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9g]]. So an "as filed" clearance with no departure instructions does not mean the hills are taken care of. You have to check for an ODP yourself [[29:39|IPH 1-23]].

check.q: How can you tell a graphic ODP from a SID?
check.a: A graphic ODP has (OBSTACLE) printed in its title [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]].

body.p: Every DP assumes three things unless it says otherwise: you cross the departure end of the runway (DER) at least 35 ft above it, you climb to 400 ft above the DER before turning, and you climb at least 200 ft/NM until reaching the minimum IFR altitude [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e1]].

The obstacle surface rises at 152 ft/NM (a 40:1 slope). Climbing at 200 ft/NM gives you at least 48 ft/NM of clearance above it [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e3]] [[29:33|IPH 1-17]]. When an obstacle sticks through that surface, the designer can require a steeper climb gradient, higher takeoff minimums so you can see the obstacle, a set route, or a mix [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9d]].

callout.text: A published climb gradient is mandatory when the procedure is part of your ATC clearance, unless increased takeoff minimums are offered and the weather lets you meet them [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e5]]. If you can't make the standard or published gradient, wait until you can depart in VMC [[29:59|IPH 1-43]].

body.p: Climb gradients are in feet per NM, but your vertical speed indicator reads feet per minute. The TPP front matter has a rate of climb table that converts gradient and groundspeed to feet per minute [[29:34|IPH 1-18]]. You can also do the math: ft/NM × groundspeed ÷ 60.

Example from the table: 297 ft/NM at 180 knots groundspeed needs 892 fpm [[29:34|IPH 1-18]]. At 90 knots the same gradient needs only 446 fpm, so a slower groundspeed makes a gradient easier to meet. Design does not consider your airplane's performance, so check it, especially at high airports on warm days [[29:34|IPH 1-18]].

head: Takeoff minimums
What the rule says
rows: 14 CFR 91.175(f) applies to Part 121, 125, 129 and 135 operators [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]]
1 SM for airplanes with two engines or less; 1/2 SM for more than two engines [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)(2)]]
Those operators must use the ODP or an ATC-assigned alternative [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)(3)]]
Not required to use takeoff minimums. A zero/zero departure is legal but never advisable [[29:24|IPH 1-8]]

body.p: Read the takeoff obstacle notes for your runway. Low, close-in obstacles are within 1 NM of the DER and do not raise the minimums [[33:351|AIM 5-2-9e4]]. To see and avoid them you may need weather of 300 ft and 1 NM or better [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f2]].

callout.text: 35, 400, 200: cross the runway end at 35 ft, no turn before 400 ft, climb at least 200 ft/NM.

check.q: The takeoff minimums say "Rwy 27, standard with a minimum climb of 280' per NM to 2500." When is that climb mandatory?
check.a: When the departure procedure is included in your ATC clearance [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e5]].

chunks.title: Flying a SID: transitions, climb via and when to say no

body.p: A SID has a basic departure and usually transition routes that fan out to the en route structure. When you file, include the transition code. The clearance names both, for example "Joe Pool Nine Departure, College Station Transition" [[29:42|IPH 1-26]].
A radar SID uses vectors from just after takeoff instead of pilot navigation, and it often has its own lost communication procedure. Review it before you go [[29:42|IPH 1-26]].

bullets: To accept a SID you need the charted procedure with you [[29:46|IPH 1-30]].
Accept or reject it based on: your climb performance, your nav accuracy, having the chart, and understanding the whole SID [[29:46|IPH 1-30]].
If you can't make the SID climb gradient, don't accept the SID, even if ATC assigns it [[29:45|IPH 1-29]].
Don't want SIDs at all? Write "NO SIDs" in the flight plan remarks [[29:42|IPH 1-26]].

head: Clearance
What you do
rows: Fly the SID lateral path and any published speed restrictions [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9h6]]
"Cleared Loop Six departure, climb and maintain four thousand."
Lateral path and speeds, climbing unrestricted to 4,000 [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9h6]]
Lateral path plus all published speed and altitude restrictions, up to the SID top altitude [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9h6]]
Same, but stop the climb at the new altitude [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9h6]]

body.p: SID altitudes come four ways: a line under the number is a minimum, a line over it is a maximum, lines over and under make it mandatory, and a number with a line over and a number with a line under is a block [[29:52|IPH 1-36]] [[29:53|IPH 1-37]].

callout.text: On "climb via," tell the next controller the altitude you're leaving and any restriction not on the chart: "Cactus Seven Eleven leaving two thousand, climbing via the Laura Two departure" [[33:357|AIM 5-2-9h7]].

Vectored off a SID? Consider it canceled, including its altitude and speed restrictions, unless ATC says "expect to resume SID" [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h3]]. Crossing altitudes and speed restrictions on an ODP, though, can't be canceled or amended by ATC [[33:358|AIM 5-2-9h9]]. If ATC vectors you off an ODP or gives you an altitude below one on it, the whole ODP is canceled and ATC takes over terrain and obstacle clearance [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h3]].

check.q: On a SID, ATC says "climb and maintain flight level two four zero" after a climb via clearance. What happens to the published altitude restrictions?
check.a: They are canceled. Keep flying the lateral path and the published speed restrictions unless ATC deletes them [[33:357|AIM 5-2-9h8]] [[33:358|AIM 5-2-9h8]].

chunks.title: Airways, RNAV routes and staying on centerline

head: Route
Altitudes
Chart and color
rows: 1,200 ft AGL (or higher) up to but not including 18,000 MSL
1,200 ft AGL (or higher) up to but not including 18,000 MSL

body.p: Unless ATC says otherwise, fly the centerline of an airway, or the direct course between the fixes on any other route [[60:482|14 CFR 91.181]]. Direct routes must be defined by fixes you can fix your position over, and those fixes become compulsory reporting points unless ATC says otherwise [[29:81|IPH 2-21]].
Turns that start at or after the fix can take you outside the airway. Lead the turn, using DME or other cockpit instruments, to stay as close as you can to the route [[33:381|AIM 5-3-5]].

In level cruise in controlled airspace, fly the altitude ATC assigned [[60:480|14 CFR 91.179(a)]]. In uncontrolled airspace below 18,000 MSL: magnetic course 0° to 179°, odd thousands; 180° to 359°, even thousands [[60:481|14 CFR 91.179(b)]].

callout.text: ATC may vector you for separation, noise or an operational advantage. If the vector takes you off a nonradar route, ATC tells you what it is for [[33:380|AIM 5-3-4c]]. Fly assigned headings promptly, and question any heading or altitude that looks wrong [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]].

check.q: You are IFR in uncontrolled airspace on a magnetic course of 200°, below 18,000 ft. Which is correct: 5,000 or 6,000 ft?
check.a: 6,000. Courses of 180° to 359° use even thousands [[60:481|14 CFR 91.179(b)]].

chunks.title: En route altitudes: MEA, MOCA, MRA, MAA, MCA and MTA

head: Altitude
What it guarantees
rows: Nav signal coverage and obstacle clearance between fixes, for the whole width of the airway [[29:95|IPH 2-35]]. Two-way radio contact is not guaranteed [[23:25|IFH 1-6]]
Obstacle clearance for the whole segment, but nav signals only within 22 NM of the VOR [[29:96|IPH 2-36]]. Charted with a leading asterisk, like *3400 [[23:25|IFH 1-6]]
Lowest altitude where you can receive the off-course NAVAID that defines a fix [[29:95|IPH 2-35]]
Highest usable altitude on the segment with good nav signals [[29:96|IPH 2-36]]
Lowest altitude to cross a fix when you're flying toward a higher MEA [[29:100|IPH 2-40]]
Higher altitude needed to turn at certain fixes, shown with the MCA flag and a note [[33:381|AIM 5-3-7]]

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.177: don't fly below the published minimum altitudes. You may go below the MEA down to the MOCA only if nav signals are available, and on VOR only within 22 NM of that VOR. Where nothing is published, stay 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of your course (2,000 ft in mountainous areas) [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]].

body.p: Going to a higher MEA, start the climb right after passing the fix where it begins. But if there is an MCA, you must already be at or above it when you cross that fix [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(b)]].

In Figure 2-62, V361 has an MEA of 5,200 then 5,900. The flag at SQWID reads "V 361 5900 E": eastbound, cross SQWID at or above 5,900 [[29:99|IPH 2-39]]. Designers set the MCA from a climb gradient that depends on the flight altitude: 150 ft/NM from sea level to 5,000 MSL, 120 ft/NM from 5,000 to 10,000 MSL, and 100 ft/NM above 10,000 MSL [[29:100|IPH 2-40]]. Pick the band for the altitudes you climb through between the fix and the obstacle.

Worked example (IPH Figure 2-63): obstruction 4,620 ft + 2,000 ft clearance = 6,620 ft needed at the obstruction. It is 6 NM past the fix, and 6 × 120 = 720 ft of climb is allowed, so the MCA is 6,620 − 720 = 5,900 ft [[29:99|IPH 2-39]].

callout.text: These minimum altitude rules apply to all IFR flights, even in VFR weather and even on a VFR-on-top clearance [[29:95|IPH 2-35]].

check.q: The MEA is 6,000 and the MOCA is *4,200. You navigate by VOR and are 30 NM from the station. Can you descend to 4,200?
check.a: No. On VOR you can use the MOCA only within 22 NM of the VOR [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(1)]].

chunks.title: Changeover points and using the right NAVAIDs

body.p: A changeover point (COP) is where you switch your nav receiver from the station behind you to the station ahead [[33:381|AIM 5-3-6a]]. It is normally midway between the two NAVAIDs. If it is not midway, the chart shows the COP and the distance to each NAVAID [[33:381|AIM 5-3-6b]].
COPs keep you from losing nav guidance at the MEA, prevent frequency interference, and make sure all aircraft in that airspace use the same stations [[33:381|AIM 5-3-6c]] [[29:81|IPH 2-21]].

bullets: Identify every NAVAID you use. VORs are identified by Morse code, voice, or both [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].
No identifier, or a T-E-S-T code, means the station is off the air for maintenance and may be unreliable even if you get a signal [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]].
Don't fly a procedure based on a NAVAID that is NOTAMed out of service, even if you hear an identifier [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]].
Arrows next to an intersection show which NAVAID identifies it. A hollow arrowhead means DME may be used [[23:29|IFH 1-10]].

callout.text: No COP on the chart? Change frequencies halfway [[23:29|IFH 1-10]].

check.q: Two VORs are 76 NM apart on an airway and no COP is charted. Where do you switch?

chunks.title: Talking to ATC en route: required reports

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.183: on IFR in controlled airspace, keep a continuous listening watch and report as soon as possible: (a) time and altitude over each designated reporting point, or only the ones ATC asks for while in radar contact; (b) any unforecast weather; and (c) anything else about the safety of flight [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183]].

14 CFR 91.187: report any in-flight failure of nav, approach or comm equipment as soon as practical. Include aircraft ID, equipment affected, how much it hurts your ability to fly IFR, and what help you want from ATC [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

body.p: Compulsory reporting points are solid triangles; open triangles are reported only on request [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2b]]. Once ATC says "radar contact," stop routine position reports. Start again when you hear "radar contact lost" or "radar service terminated" [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2c3]].

A position report gives: ID, position, time, altitude, type of flight plan (not needed when talking to ARTCC or approach), ETA and name of the next reporting point, name of the one after, and remarks [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2d]] [[33:377|AIM 5-3-2d]].

head: Report without being asked (AIM 5-3-3)
When
rows: Leaving an assigned altitude for a new one
Can't climb or descend at 500 fpm or more
TAS changes 5% or 10 knots (whichever is greater) from the flight plan
Reaching a holding fix (time and altitude) and leaving it
Loss of VOR, ADF, ILS, GPS anomalies, or comm trouble
Leaving the FAF (or outer marker) inbound
A corrected estimate if the old one is off by more than 2 minutes

body.p: Center frequencies are for controlling IFR traffic. Get en route weather and similar data from Flight Service [[33:359|AIM 5-3-1a]]. If a center frequency seems dead, wait at least 1 minute, then try the last controller, another center frequency, or Flight Service [[33:375|AIM 5-3-1c]].

callout.text: On first contact with a new controller, give your altitude so they can check your Mode C: "Birmingham Departure, Cessna 1230A climbing through 2,700" [[23:323|IFH 10-32]]. Read back altitudes, vectors and runways [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b]].

check.q: Your VOR receiver fails in IMC but GPS still works. What four items go in your report to ATC?
check.a: Aircraft ID, equipment affected, degree your IFR capability is impaired, and the help you want from ATC [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(b)]].

chunks.title: Arrivals: STARs, descend via and crossing restrictions

body.p: A STAR is an ATC-coded IFR arrival route. It simplifies clearances and links the en route structure to the approach [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a]]. It usually ends at a fix where you get vectors or join an approach [[29:124|IPH 3-12]]. STARs typically use a descent of about 318 ft/NM (about 3°) [[29:124|IPH 3-12]].

bullets: You need at least the approved chart to use a STAR. RNAV STARs must be retrievable by name from the database [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1c]].
Don't want STARs? Put "NO STAR" in the remarks [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1c]].
"Expect" altitudes and speeds are for planning only. They are not restrictions until ATC says them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]].
Published speed restrictions are mandatory unless ATC changes them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]].
MEAs on a STAR aren't restrictions, but stay above them unless ATC clears you lower [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]].

head: Clearance
What you do
rows: Lateral path and published speeds only. No descent [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]]
"Cleared Tyler One arrival, descend and maintain FL 240."
Descend to FL 240 and hold it until cleared further [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]]
Descend at your discretion, meeting all published altitude and speed restrictions [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]]
"Descend via ..., except after Geeno, maintain one zero thousand."
Fly it as published to Geeno, then stop at 10,000 until cleared [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]]

callout.text: With a STAR in your route, keep your last assigned altitude until ATC authorizes descent. Vectored off a STAR? It and its restrictions are canceled [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]]. On each new frequency say: altitude leaving, "descending via (name)," the runway transition if assigned, and any extra restrictions [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1a2b]].

body.p: **Descent clearances.** "Descend and maintain" means start down promptly: an optimum rate until 1,000 ft above the altitude, then 500 to 1,500 fpm [[29:121|IPH 3-9]]. "At pilot's discretion" lets you start when you want and level off on the way, but once you leave an altitude you may not go back to it [[29:121|IPH 3-9]].

Plan the descent so you reach the crossing altitude without diving. IPH example: 11,000 ft down to 3,000 ft at ECA VOR, 1,000 fpm, 180 knots groundspeed [[29:120|IPH 3-8]]. That is 8,000 ft ÷ 1,000 fpm = 8 minutes. At 3 NM per minute, start down 24 NM before ECA.

callout.text: Accepting a direct clearance off airways means you share the responsibility for terrain clearance. Know the highest terrain and obstacles around you [[29:121|IPH 3-9]].

check.q: You hear "Cleared HADLY ONE arrival." May you start down to the first published altitude on the STAR?
check.a: No. That clearance is for the lateral route only [[29:124|IPH 3-12]] [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]].

chunks.title: Using GPS and RNAV on departures, en route and arrivals

bullets: Only IFR-approved GPS may be used for IFR. VFR and hand-held units are not authorized [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].
With un-augmented GPS (TSO-C129 or C196), you also need another approved nav system for the route, like VOR [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].
The database must be current. Check its dates before flight, and check that waypoint names and order match the chart in flight [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]] [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17]].
RNAV procedures must be loaded by name from the current database, not built waypoint by waypoint [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16a2]].
Load RNAV routes (T or Q) whole when you can [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16a3]].

head: Phase
GPS CDI full-scale
rows: ±1 NM, with the route from the database [[33:94|AIM 1-1-17]]
Within 30 NM of the destination with the approach armed

body.p: Public PBN SIDs are normally RNAV 1, RNP 1 or A-RNP. RNAV 1 and RNP 1 require total system error of no more than 1 NM for 95% of the flight time [[33:358|AIM 5-2-9i1]]. RNAV STARs are RNAV 1 or RNAV 2, shown in the chart notes [[29:124|IPH 3-12]]. Items listed in the PBN box on the chart are required [[33:358|AIM 5-2-9i2]]. On RNAV 1 STARs you must use a CDI, flight director, or autopilot in LNAV mode [[29:124|IPH 3-12]].

Fly-by waypoints (a four-pointed star) let you start the turn early. Fly-over waypoints (the star in a circle) must be crossed before you turn. Don't change a waypoint's type in the database [[29:52|IPH 1-36]].

A suitable IFR GPS can substitute for an out-of-service VOR, DME or NDB, or replace ADF or DME you don't have, on conventional routes. You may need to tell ATC [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3a]] [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]].

callout.text: Check RAIM before a GPS departure. If RAIM is predicted to be out, use other nav equipment, reroute, delay or cancel [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]] [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17]]. If GPS fails, tell ATC "unable RNAV" and ask for an amended clearance [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16a1]].

check.q: What CDI sensitivity must your GPS be set to for a published RNAV departure?
check.a: Terminal, ±1 NM, using the route from the database [[33:94|AIM 1-1-17]].

chunks.title: Weather in flight and digital displays

body.p: Keep updating the weather. Ask Flight Service for destination and en route weather, and give a PIREP when you can [[23:323|IFH 10-32]]. Report unforecast weather, or forecast hazardous weather, to ATC [[33:378|AIM 5-3-3b]] [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183(b)]].

FIS-B sends weather and aeronautical information to your cockpit display over ADS-B. It does not replace a preflight briefing or in-flight updates from Flight Service or ATC, and it should not be your only source [[33:306|AIM 4-5-9]].

head: Display
Know this limit
rows: NEXRAD on an app or uplink
5 to 15 minutes or more old. Use it only for broad, strategic avoidance, never to pick through storms [[28:25|AWH 3-2]]
Shows where precipitation was. It may be 15 to 20 minutes older than the time shown [[28:327|AWH 24-43]]
Check its time or "valid until" stamp [[28:25|AWH 3-2]]

callout.text: Prefer to stay on top of a cloud layer longer, for example to avoid icing? Ask for a descent at pilot's discretion [[29:121|IPH 3-9]].

check.q: Your tablet's NEXRAD image is stamped 2 minutes ago. How old could the weather really be?
check.a: Older than shown: a datalinked mosaic may be 15 to 20 minutes older than the indicated age [[28:327|AWH 24-43]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: from clearance to the arrival

body.p: **Before takeoff** (IFH example flight [[23:322|IFH 10-31]]):

bullets: 1. Check you have current charts or a current EFB. EFB data used for navigation must be current and verified by you [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]].
2. Look up the takeoff minimums, ODP and obstacle notes for your runway. Check that you can make any climb gradient [[34:9|AIM 5-5-14]] [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9h]].
3. Copy the clearance, read it back and review the DP [[23:322|IFH 10-31]] [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7a]].
4. Tune and identify radios, set up nav equipment, and load the flight plan in the GPS [[23:322|IFH 10-31]].
5. Before-takeoff checklist and run-up. On the runway: heading indicator matches the compass, transponder on, lights and pitot heat on [[23:322|IFH 10-31]] [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].

body.p: **Departure and en route:**

bullets: 6. Fly the DP: 400 ft before turning unless the DP says higher, then each turn and crossing altitude as published [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e1]].
7. Don't switch to departure until told. Then give your altitude on first call [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8c]] [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].
8. Intercept each course or radial promptly and lead turns at fixes [[33:381|AIM 5-3-5]]. Switch VORs at the COP [[33:381|AIM 5-3-6]].
9. Note the time at each fix to track progress [[23:323|IFH 10-32]]. Record fuel at top of climb and along the route [[29:112|IPH 2-52]].
10. Make the required reports and update the weather [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]] [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].

body.p: **Arrival:** get ATIS early, review the STAR and approach, check fuel, and finish landing checklists early so you can concentrate on the approach [[29:128|IPH 3-16]].

head: ACS standard
Tolerance
rows: No more than ¾-scale CDI deflection (ACS IR.V.B.S7)

callout.text: SRM: before flight, organize frequencies, charts and diversion airports so you can act like a crew of one when something breaks [[30:57|RMH 8-4]]. Resources are inside and outside the airplane: ATC is one, and installed equipment you know how to use well is another [[30:56|RMH 8-3]].

check.q: On a SID with a speed restriction at a waypoint, when may you speed up?

body.p: **ATC communications and compliance (R1).** Once you have a clearance, don't deviate unless you get an amended clearance, have an emergency, or are following a TCAS resolution advisory. If unsure, ask right away [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]. You may refuse a clearance you can't fly safely [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7c]].

callout.text: IPH example: an MD-80 crew read back 5,000 ft when cleared to 7,000, the controller missed it, and they descended toward mountains until GPWS and ATC warnings. Hurried or nonstandard phraseology has been a factor in many CFIT accidents [[29:121|IPH 3-9]].

bullets: Read back altitudes, restrictions and vectors in the order given, with your call sign [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b]].
Don't read back altitudes printed on a DP or approach unless the controller says them [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b]].
"Radar contact" does not relieve you of terrain and obstacle clearance, which may mean flying the ODP [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]].

body.p: **Limits of traffic equipment (R2).**

head: System
Limitation
rows: Not all aircraft have ADS-B Out or a transponder, so some won't show [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]]. Not a collision avoidance system; no avoidance maneuvers in IMC based on it [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]]
Shows only transponder-equipped aircraft, updates every 3 to 13 seconds, and needs radar coverage; you can't tell if you're getting it [[33:305|AIM 4-5-8]] [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8d]]
Proximity warning only, to help you see traffic. No avoidance maneuvers [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16a]]
Not on all traffic. Some aircraft aren't on radar, and controllers may be busy [[34:7|AIM 5-5-10]]

body.p: Deviating from your clearance for traffic on a TIS-B display needs ATC approval first, unless there is an imminent emergency. Other aircraft you can't see on your screen may be nearby [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8d]].

**See and avoid (R3).** When the weather permits, you must see and avoid other traffic, terrain and obstacles, no matter your flight plan or radar service [[34:6|AIM 5-5-8]]. Even on an IFR flight plan, you are still responsible for seeing and avoiding other aircraft [[23:323|IFH 10-32]]. Limit time on instruments and tablets, and scan the whole sky [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

callout.text: Screens help you find traffic. Eyes avoid it. ATC approves any deviation in IMC.

check.q: In IMC your ADS-B display shows traffic converging at your altitude. What do you do?
check.a: Don't maneuver based on the display. Tell ATC and ask for help or a vector [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]] [[34:7|AIM 5-5-10]].

bullets: Assuming an "as filed" clearance protects you from terrain without checking for an ODP [[29:39|IPH 1-23]] [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]].
Turning before 400 ft above the runway end or before the DP's turn point [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e1]].
Accepting a SID or DP climb gradient the airplane can't make [[29:45|IPH 1-29]].
Treating "cleared (STAR) arrival" as permission to descend [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]].
Flying "expect" altitudes as if they were restrictions, or using them after lost comms [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]].
Descending to the MOCA more than 22 NM from the VOR [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(1)]].
Climbing toward a higher MEA without checking for an MCA [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(b)]].
Forgetting to report leaving an altitude, or a TAS change of 5% or 10 knots [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1]].
Building an RNAV procedure from loose waypoints instead of loading it by name [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16a2]].
Heads-down on displays and missing traffic in VMC [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

check.q: Why is "climbing to the next MEA right after the fix" sometimes wrong?
check.a: If an MCA is published, you must already be at or above it when you cross the fix [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(b)]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: MEA gaps, MCA and MTA boxes, and crossing restrictions

body.p: A gap in signal coverage is flagged on the airway. The longest gap allowed grows with altitude. On the IPH graph, enter the MEA on the left and read the gap across the bottom. The sample shows 13,000 ft gives about 18.5 NM [[29:89|IPH p 89]] [[29:90|IPH Figure 2-49]]. The chart does not mark where the gap starts and ends, so plan to dead reckon through it.

An MCA box lists the airway, altitude and direction letter. At JACKSON the yellow box reads V520 14600 W and V330 13200 W. A red MTA box covers turns: V330 E to V520 W 16000 means you need 16,000 ft before you start that turn [[29:97|IPH Figure 2-59]]. You must be at or above the MTA before beginning the turn [[29:98|IPH p 98]].

A STAR can add crossing restrictions. On the PENNS TWO ARRIVAL, RACKI to PENNS is 23 NM and you cross PENNS at 6,000 ft. At 180 knots (3 NM per minute) from 12,000 ft at RACKI, that is about 8 minutes, so you need at least 750 fpm [[29:132|IPH Figure 3-17]].

The method is simple. Distance divided by groundspeed gives minutes. Altitude to lose divided by minutes gives the descent rate. Do the math before the fix, then check it against your climb or descent capability [[29:132|IPH Figure 3-17]].

scenario.title: Out of the hills, across the airways, into the arrival
scenario.setup: You are departing IFR alone in a single-engine airplane from a nontowered airport in hilly terrain. The ceiling is 600 overcast. The TPP lists for your runway: takeoff minimums "1500-3 or standard with a minimum climb of 350' per NM to 4000," plus a textual ODP. Your POH shows you can climb at about 500 fpm at a groundspeed of 90 knots. Later en route you will fly a Victor airway in and out of radar coverage, and arrive on a STAR.

questions.q: Can you take off under IFR today, and why?
questions.a: Not safely or by the procedure. 350 ft/NM at 90 knots needs about 525 fpm (350 × 90 ÷ 60), more than your 500 fpm. The other option, 1500-3, is above the 600 ft ceiling. If you can't make the gradient, wait until you can depart in VMC [[29:59|IPH 1-43]]. A gradient is mandatory when the procedure is in your clearance unless higher minimums are offered and the weather meets them [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e5]].

questions.q: The next day you depart. Center says "radar contact," and an hour later "radar service terminated." What changes for you?
questions.a: You must now give position reports over each compulsory reporting point (solid triangle) [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2c]]. Include ID, position, time, altitude, ETA and name of the next point, the name of the one after, and remarks [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2d]] [[33:377|AIM 5-3-2d]]. Also report leaving the FAF inbound, and fix any estimate that is off by more than 2 minutes [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a2]].

questions.q: In the clouds, your ADS-B display shows a target 2 miles ahead at your altitude, closing. What do you do?
questions.a: Don't turn or climb based on the display alone. ADS-B is not a collision avoidance system and must not be used for avoidance maneuvers in IMC [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]]. Tell ATC and ask for a vector if needed [[34:7|AIM 5-5-10]]. Remember some aircraft won't show at all [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

questions.q: You break out between layers in clear air. ATC is giving you traffic calls. Is watching for traffic still your job?
questions.a: Yes. When the weather permits, you must see and avoid other traffic, terrain and obstacles on any flight plan, even under radar control [[34:6|AIM 5-5-8]]. ATC may not call all traffic [[34:7|AIM 5-5-10]].

questions.q: You hit light icing that wasn't forecast. What must you do?
questions.a: Report it to ATC as soon as possible: unforecast weather is a required report [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183(b)]] [[33:378|AIM 5-3-3b]]. Then get updated weather from Flight Service and decide whether to change altitude or route [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].

questions.q: Approach says "descend via the arrival" and switches you. You realize you're not sure whether the next fix is "at" or "at or above." What now?
questions.a: Check the chart, and if still uncertain, ask ATC right away [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]. On the new frequency, state your altitude leaving and "descending via" the STAR name [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1a2b]].

skills.do: Pick, tune and identify the NAVAIDs and frequencies for the departure, route and arrival, including COP frequency changes.
skills.practice: On a training flight, identify each VOR by Morse code before using it [[23:254|IFH 9-11]], and switch at each charted COP or midway [[33:381|AIM 5-3-6]].

skills.do: Complete the checklist items for each phase: before takeoff, climb, cruise, descent and before landing.
skills.practice: Run your POH checklists and the IFR items from the IFH example: pitot heat, transponder on, heading indicator set to the compass [[23:323|IFH 10-32]]. Finish landing checklists early on the arrival [[29:128|IPH 3-16]].

skills.do: Use current paper or electronic charts and a current GPS database for the DP, route and STAR.
skills.practice: Before each flight, check EFB chart dates [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]] and the GPS database dates, and compare loaded waypoints with the chart [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]] [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17]].

skills.do: Contact the right facility, use proper phraseology and comply promptly with ATC instructions and airspace restrictions.
skills.practice: Practice first calls with altitude [[23:323|IFH 10-32]], readbacks in the order given [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b]], and "climbing via" and "descending via" reports [[33:357|AIM 5-2-9h7]] [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1a2b]].

skills.do: Intercept all courses, radials and bearings for the procedure, route or clearance in a timely way.
skills.practice: Lead turns at fixes using DME or GPS so you stay on the airway [[33:381|AIM 5-3-5]]. Use terminal ±1 NM CDI sensitivity on DPs [[33:94|AIM 1-1-17]].

skills.do: Comply with all charted procedures: DP turns and crossing altitudes, climb gradients, STAR speeds and altitudes.
skills.practice: Brief each DP and STAR out loud: turn altitude, gradient, restrictions and top or bottom altitude [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e1]] [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]].

skills.do: Hold airspeed ±10 knots, altitude ±100 ft and selected headings ±10°, and keep the CDI within ¾-scale deflection (ACS IR.V.B.S7).
skills.practice: Trim before any chart or GPS work. Report a TAS change of 5% or 10 knots from your flight plan [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1]].

skills.do: Update and interpret weather in flight.
skills.practice: Call Flight Service for destination and en route weather and give a PIREP on each training cross-country [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].

skills.do: Use digital weather and aeronautical information displays to keep situational awareness.
skills.practice: Read the time stamp on every FIS-B product. Use NEXRAD only for strategic avoidance [[28:25|AWH 3-2]] [[33:306|AIM 4-5-9]].
Before flight, list diversion airports with frequencies and approaches, and decide which resources, such as ATC and your installed equipment, you'll use when [[30:56|RMH 8-3]] [[30:57|RMH 8-4]].

quiz.q: Which departure procedure may you fly without an ATC clearance, as long as ATC hasn't assigned something else?
options: A SID
A radar SID
An ODP
An RNAV SID
quiz.why: ODPs may be flown without ATC clearance unless ATC assigns a SID or radar vectors. SIDs always need a clearance [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a]].

quiz.q: Unless a DP says otherwise, obstacle protection assumes you:
options: Cross the runway end at 35 ft, climb to 400 ft before turning, climb 200 ft/NM
Cross the runway end at 50 ft, climb to 500 ft before turning, and climb 152 ft/NM
Cross the runway end at 35 ft, turn as soon as you reach 200 ft, and climb 300 ft/NM
Climb 500 fpm until reaching 1,000 ft above the airport
quiz.why: The standard is 35 ft over the DER, 400 ft before the first turn, and at least 200 ft/NM to the minimum IFR altitude [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e1]]. 152 ft/NM is the slope of the obstacle surface, not your climb [[33:350|AIM 5-2-9e3]].

options: Every pilot departing under IFR
Only airports with no published ODP
Only airplanes departing under IFR at night
Part 121, 125, 129 and 135 operators
quiz.why: 91.175(f) says it applies to persons operating under Parts 121, 125, 129 or 135 [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]]. Part 91 pilots are not required to use them, though it is wise [[29:24|IPH 1-8]].

quiz.q: Using the rate of climb table, what climb rate meets 297 ft/NM at a 120 knot groundspeed?
options: 446 fpm
892 fpm
595 fpm
297 fpm
quiz.why: The table shows 595 fpm for 297 ft/NM at 120 knots [[29:34|IPH 1-18]]. Check: 297 × 120 ÷ 60 = 594. 892 fpm is the 180 knot value.

quiz.q: A route segment shows MEA 7,000 and *5,500. What does the 5,500 guarantee?
options: Obstacle clearance, with nav signals only within 22 NM of the VOR
Obstacle clearance plus navigation signals along the whole segment
Obstacle clearance plus two-way radio contact with ATC along the segment
Reliable reception of the off-course NAVAID that defines a fix on the segment
quiz.why: The asterisk marks the MOCA: obstacle clearance for the whole segment, nav signals only within 22 NM of the VOR [[29:96|IPH 2-36]] [[23:25|IFH 1-6]]. Receiving an off-course NAVAID is the MRA.

quiz.q: ATC tells you "radar contact." What happens to your position reports?
options: Make them only at the non-compulsory open-triangle reporting points
Keep making them at every compulsory reporting point along the route
Stop them until ATC says radar contact lost or service terminated
Make them every 30 minutes until the controller hands you off
quiz.why: In radar contact, stop position reports over designated points and resume when ATC says "radar contact lost" or "radar service terminated" [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2c3]].

quiz.q: You hear "Cleared Tyler One arrival." What are you cleared to do?
options: Descend via all of the STAR's published altitudes and speed restrictions
Fly the lateral path and published speeds, with no descent
Descend at pilot's discretion to the lowest published altitude on the STAR
Proceed direct to the airport and descend as needed for the approach
quiz.why: That is a lateral routing clearance only. You comply with published speeds, but no descent is authorized [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]].

quiz.q: Which aircraft will NOT appear as TIS-B traffic on your display?
options: An airplane with a Mode C transponder in radar coverage
An airplane with a Mode S transponder in radar coverage
An airplane with no transponder
An airliner on an IFR flight plan
quiz.why: TIS-B only uplinks transponder-equipped aircraft. Aircraft without a transponder are not shown [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8d]].

quiz.q: Climbing to a higher MEA with no MCA published, when do you start the climb?
options: Right after passing the fix where the higher MEA begins
About 5 NM before the fix, so you cross it at the higher MEA
Whenever ATC reminds you, since ATC controls all climbs on airways
Halfway along the new segment, so you reach the new MEA by its end
quiz.why: Begin the climb immediately after passing the point where the higher minimum applies. With an MCA, you must cross the fix at or above it [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(b)]].

quiz.q: On the graph, enter with an MEA of 13,000 ft. What allowable gap does the sample show?
quiz.why: The sample reads: enter with MEA of 13,000 feet, read allowable gap 18.5 NM [[29:90|IPH Figure 2-49]].

quiz.q: On the graph, as the MEA gets higher, the allowable gap:
options: Is always zero
Stays the same
Gets longer
Gets shorter
quiz.why: The line rises to the right, so the allowed gap grows with altitude [[29:89|IPH p 89]] [[29:90|IPH Figure 2-49]].

quiz.q: You are westbound on V330 at JACKSON. What is the MCA in the yellow box?
quiz.why: The yellow box reads V330 13200 W. 14,600 ft is for V520 westbound [[29:97|IPH Figure 2-59]].

quiz.q: You turn at this fix from V330 eastbound to V520 westbound. What is the lowest altitude you may fly (the MTA)?
quiz.why: The MTA box reads V330 E to V520 W 16000 [[29:97|IPH Figure 2-59]].

quiz.q: At RACKI at 12,000 ft you have 23 NM to PENNS, 180 knots groundspeed, and must cross at 6,000 ft. What is the least descent rate?
options: 750 fpm
500 fpm
quiz.why: 23 NM at 3 NM per minute is about 8 minutes. 6,000 ft divided by 8 is 750 fpm [[29:132|IPH Figure 3-17]].

takeaways: Before every IFR departure, look up the takeoff minimums, ODP and obstacle notes. "As filed" does not mean protected.
35, 400, 200: cross the runway end at 35 ft, no turn below 400 ft, climb at least 200 ft/NM. Convert ft/NM to fpm with groundspeed.
SIDs and STARs need a clearance and a current chart. "Climb via" and "descend via" add the published altitudes; without them you fly the lateral path only.
MEA: signals and obstacles. MOCA: obstacles, signals only within 22 NM. MCA: cross the fix at or above it.
Report without being asked: leaving altitudes, unforecast weather, equipment failures (91.183, 91.187, AIM 5-3-3).
Traffic displays help you look. They don't clear you to maneuver in IMC. In VMC, see and avoid is always yours.
cfi_notes: The IFH says to give a corrected estimate when the old one is off by more than 3 minutes [[23:299|IFH 10-8]]. The current AIM says more than 2 minutes (3 minutes only in the North Atlantic) [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a2]]. Teach the AIM.

The IFH points to "paragraph 5-2-7 of the AIM" for DPs [[23:296|IFH 10-5]]. In the current AIM it is paragraph 5-2-9 [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9]]. The IFH and IPH also use older names like AFSS and AeroNav Products.

Examiners often ask whether Part 91 must follow takeoff minimums. 91.175(f) applies to Parts 121, 125, 129 and 135 [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]]. Have students explain why zero/zero is legal but unwise [[29:24|IPH 1-8]], and who owns obstacle clearance when no ODP is filed or assigned [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f1]].

Make students convert every published gradient to fpm at their own climb groundspeed, using the TPP table [[29:34|IPH 1-18]]. A headwind lowers groundspeed and makes the gradient easier; a tailwind makes it harder.

Students confuse "cleared (STAR) arrival" with "descend via." Drill the AIM example clearances until they can say what each allows [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]], and the matching ones for SIDs [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9h6]].
Use the IPH MD-80 readback story to show why readbacks and "say again" matter [[29:121|IPH 3-9]].
IPH and IFH chart figures are 2005 to 2010 samples marked not for navigation. Brief real, current DPs and STARs from your home airport and nearby airports.

Note the dates: the IPH says to check RAIM before RNAV departures with TSO-C129 GPS [[29:46|IPH 1-30]]; the current AIM also asks for a RAIM prediction for a published GPS departure [[33:97|AIM 1-1-17]].
gaps: Climb performance, fuel burn and checklists for the training airplane come from its POH/AFM, which is not in these sources.
How to load and fly SIDs, STARs and airways on a specific GPS navigator or autopilot comes from the avionics manual, not these sources.
AC 90-100A and AC 90-105 (RNAV and RNP operations) are not available here; RNAV content is taught from the AIM and IPH.
One-engine-inoperative takeoff obstacle clearance (Part 121/135, 91.175(f)(4)) is multiengine and commercial-operator content and is only mentioned, not taught.
Current IFR en route chart symbols are only covered briefly from the IFH text; the Chart Users' Guide IFR section was not used for this lesson.

activities.title: ODP or SID?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: May be flown without an ATC clearance
Designed for ATC flow and less radio talk
Graphic version has (OBSTACLE) in its title
Its altitude restrictions can't be canceled by ATC

activities.title: Work the numbers: gradients, descents and reports
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: An ODP requires a minimum climb of 350 ft/NM. Your climb groundspeed is 100 knots. What climb rate in feet per minute do you need?
items.why: 350 × 100 ÷ 60 = 583 fpm. The TPP rate of climb table makes the same conversion from gradient and groundspeed [[29:34|IPH 1-18]].

items.q: IPH example: an obstacle is 2,049 ft MSL, the climb starts at 1,221 ft MSL, and the obstacle is 3.1 NM from the DER. Using CG = (O − E) ÷ (0.76 × D), what climb gradient is required (round up)?
You must cross a fix at 4,000 ft. You are at 10,000 ft, plan 750 fpm down, and expect a 150 knot groundspeed. How many NM before the fix should you start down?
items.why: 6,000 ft ÷ 750 fpm = 8 minutes. 150 knots = 2.5 NM per minute, so 8 × 2.5 = 20 NM. Plan descents to arrive at the crossing altitude [[29:120|IPH 3-8]].

items.q: You fly an MEA of 3,500 ft toward a higher MEA in a mountainous area. An obstacle 4 NM past the fix is 2,600 ft MSL and needs 2,000 ft of clearance. The whole climb stays below 5,000 ft MSL, so use the IPH gradient for sea level to 5,000 ft MSL. What is the MCA?
items.why: 2,600 + 2,000 = 4,600 ft needed at the obstacle. From sea level to 5,000 ft MSL the gradient is 150 ft/NM, so 4 × 150 = 600 ft. 4,600 − 600 = 4,000 ft, and the climb from 4,000 to 4,600 stays in that band [[29:100|IPH 2-40]] [[29:99|IPH 2-39]].

items.q: You filed a TAS of 220 knots. What is the smallest change in TAS, in knots, that you must report to ATC?
items.why: Report a change of 5% or 10 knots, whichever is greater. 5% of 220 is 11 knots, which is greater than 10 [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1]].

activities.title: Name that en route altitude
activities.intro: Tap an altitude, then what it guarantees.

pairs.r: Nav signals and obstacle clearance between fixes
Obstacle clearance; signals only within 22 NM of the VOR
Lowest altitude to receive the NAVAID that defines a fix
Highest usable altitude on the segment
Cross the fix at or above this toward a higher MEA
Higher altitude needed to turn at certain fixes

activities.title: Read the changeover point picture
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Distance from the COP to the VOR behind

activities.why: At the COP you switch from the VOR behind you to the one ahead, so you keep navigation guidance at the MEA. A COP that is not midway is charted with the mileage to each NAVAID: here 45 NM back to the VOR behind and 22 NM to the one ahead [[33:381|AIM 5-3-6]] [[29:81|IPH 2-21]].

activities.title: Build a position report
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Type of flight plan (if not talking to ARTCC or approach)
ETA and name of the next reporting point
Name only of the next succeeding reporting point

activities.title: True or false: climb via and descend via
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: "Expect" altitudes on a STAR are crossing restrictions you must meet.
cards.why: No. They are for planning only and become restrictions only if ATC says them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]].

cards.s: If ATC vectors you off a STAR, the STAR and its altitude and speed restrictions are canceled.
cards.why: Yes. ATC will give you an altitude and, if needed, a speed [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]].

cards.s: Published speed restrictions on a STAR are mandatory unless ATC changes them.
cards.why: Yes. They are independent of altitude restrictions [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]].

cards.s: After "climb via SID," ATC says "climb and maintain one zero thousand." You must still meet the SID's published altitude restrictions.
cards.why: No. A new altitude from ATC cancels the published altitude restrictions. Speed restrictions and the lateral path still apply [[33:357|AIM 5-2-9h8]].

cards.s: With a descent "at pilot's discretion," you may level off on the way down and then climb back to an altitude you already left.
cards.why: No. You may level off, but once you leave an altitude you may not return to it [[29:121|IPH 3-9]].

cards.s: To accept a STAR you need at least the approved chart.
cards.why: Yes. RNAV STARs must also be retrievable by name from the database [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1c]].

activities.title: Decide: hills, airways and a STAR
activities.intro: You are flying N123AB, a single-engine airplane, IFR alone from a nontowered airport in hilly terrain. The ceiling is 800 overcast. Your runway has a textual ODP: "climb heading 090 to 2,500 before turning." Your clearance is "as filed, climb and maintain 6,000."

steps.s: You line up for takeoff. ATC gave no departure instructions. How do you leave the airport?
options: Fly the ODP and tell ATC you are using it
Turn on course once you pass 400 ft above the runway
Stay under the clouds and turn on course visually
Climb straight ahead until ATC gives you a vector
steps.why: With no ODP, SID or vectors assigned, obstacle clearance is yours [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f1]]. Fly the ODP and tell ATC so they can separate traffic [[29:39|IPH 1-23]].

steps.s: Climbing through 4,000, Center says "radar contact." Your next fix is a compulsory reporting point. What about the position report there?
options: Give a full position report over the fix, as the compulsory point requires
Report only the time over the fix and your altitude to Center
Report it to Flight Service instead of Center, since you are climbing
Skip it; in radar contact you stop position reports
steps.why: In radar contact, stop position reports over designated points until ATC says "radar contact lost" or "radar service terminated" [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2c3]].

steps.s: Level at 6,000 you pick up icing that was not forecast. The MEA here is 5,000. What do you do?
options: Descend to 5,000 on your own, since it is the MEA
Report the icing to ATC and request a lower altitude
Say nothing and turn on the pitot heat
Turn back toward the departure airport and explain later
steps.why: Unforecast weather is a required report [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183(b)]]. Don't leave your assigned altitude without an amended clearance unless it is an emergency [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

steps.s: Near the destination ATC says "Cleared ABCDE One arrival." The first fix on the STAR shows 5,000. You are at 6,000.
options: Descend to 5,000 now to meet the published altitude
Fly the STAR's lateral path at 6,000 until cleared lower
Descend at pilot's discretion to the STAR's bottom altitude
Ask ATC to cancel the STAR
steps.why: That is a lateral routing clearance only. Keep the last assigned altitude until ATC authorizes descent [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]] [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]].

steps.s: Next: "Descend via the ABCDE One arrival, contact Approach." What is your first call to Approach?
options: "Approach, N123AB, with you on the ABCDE One arrival"
"Approach, N123AB, level at 6,000, request lower altitude on the arrival"
"Approach, N123AB, leaving 6,000, descending via ABCDE One"
"Approach, N123AB, cleared to descend via the ABCDE One arrival, with you"
steps.why: On a new frequency, state the altitude you are leaving and "descending via" the procedure name, plus any runway transition or extra restrictions [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1a2b]].

activities.title: Read the MCA and MTA boxes
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.
activities.why: The yellow box lists MCAs and the red box lists the MTA. The VORTAC sits in the compass rose, and the airways are labeled V330 and V520 [[29:97|IPH Figure 2-59]].

final_quiz.q: You depart IFR under Part 91 from a runway with a published ODP. You didn't file it, ATC didn't assign a SID or vectors, and your clearance is "as filed." Who is responsible for obstacle clearance?
options: The controller, once you are in radar contact
The procedure designer, because a diverse departure is assumed
The tower, because it issued the takeoff clearance
You, the pilot
final_quiz.why: Obstacle clearance rests with the Part 91 pilot who departs IFR without filing or being cleared for an ODP, SID or DVA headings [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f1]]. "Radar contact" does not relieve you of it [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]].

final_quiz.q: Takeoff minimums read "Rwy 12, 400-2 1/2 or std. w/min. climb of 261' per NM to 500." The weather is 300 overcast. Your climb groundspeed is 90 knots. What climb rate do you need?
options: About 523 fpm
About 261 fpm
About 392 fpm
About 200 fpm
final_quiz.why: With the ceiling below 400, the 400-2 1/2 option is out, so the climb gradient option is the one that keeps you clear of the obstacles. That gradient is mandatory when the procedure is part of your ATC clearance [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e5]]. 261 × 90 ÷ 60 = 391.5, about 392 fpm. The TPP rate of climb table does the same conversion [[29:34|IPH 1-18]].

final_quiz.q: ATC assigns you a SID with a climb gradient your airplane can't make with today's weight and temperature. What should you do?
options: Accept it and climb as best you can
Accept it and ask for a lower altitude after takeoff
Accept it, since ATC is responsible for obstacle clearance on a SID
Don't accept it, and ask for another departure
final_quiz.why: If you can't comply with a SID's climb gradient, you must not accept the procedure, even when ATC assigns it [[29:45|IPH 1-29]]. You are the one who accepts or rejects a SID [[29:46|IPH 1-30]].

final_quiz.q: Your clearance is "Cleared Loop Six departure, climb and maintain four thousand." The SID has an "at or below 3,000" restriction at the first fix. What do you do?
options: Level off at 3,000 until you cross the fix, then continue the climb to 4,000
Ask for vectors, because the SID can't be flown without a "climb via" clearance
Climb to the SID top altitude while meeting every altitude and speed restriction
Fly the lateral path and published speeds, climbing unrestricted to 4,000
final_quiz.why: Without "climb via," this clearance means comply with the lateral path and published speed restrictions while climbing unrestricted to 4,000 [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9h6]].

final_quiz.q: You fly a segment with MEA 5,000 and MOCA *3,400, navigating by VOR. You are 30 NM from the VOR and want to get under icing. What is the lowest altitude you may fly without other ATC authorization?
final_quiz.why: On VOR, you may use the MOCA only within 22 NM of that VOR. At 30 NM the MEA of 5,000 applies [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(1)]] [[29:96|IPH 2-36]].

final_quiz.q: An airway's MEA rises from 6,000 to a higher value at a fix. Past the fix, an obstacle at 5,200 ft MSL in a mountainous area is 5 NM away and needs 2,000 ft of clearance. Using the IPH gradient for 5,000 to 10,000 ft MSL, what MCA results?
final_quiz.why: 5,200 + 2,000 = 7,200 ft needed at the obstacle. The climb from the MCA up to 7,200 is in the 5,000 to 10,000 ft MSL band, where the gradient is 120 ft/NM, so 5 × 120 = 600 ft. 7,200 − 600 = 6,600 ft, the same method as IPH Figure 2-63 [[29:100|IPH 2-40]] [[29:99|IPH 2-39]]. 6,450 wrongly uses 150 ft/NM.

final_quiz.q: Two VORs on your airway are 80 NM apart. The chart shows no changeover point. Where do you switch from the VOR behind you to the one ahead?
options: At 22 NM from the first VOR
40 NM from the first VOR
Whenever the first needle starts to wander
Over the second VOR
final_quiz.why: The COP is normally midway; only a COP that is not midway is charted [[33:381|AIM 5-3-6b]]. Halfway is 40 NM. 22 NM is the MOCA signal limit, not a COP.

final_quiz.q: You filed a true airspeed of 160 knots. At cruise, which actual TAS requires a report to ATC?
options: 155 knots
148 knots
153 knots
167 knots
final_quiz.why: Report a TAS change of 5% or 10 knots, whichever is greater [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1]]. 5% of 160 is 8, so the threshold is 10 knots. 148 is 12 knots slow; the others are within 10.

final_quiz.q: Your only VOR receiver fails in IMC. Which list matches what 91.187 requires in your report?
options: Aircraft ID, equipment affected, degree of IFR impairment, and help wanted
Aircraft ID, fuel remaining, souls on board, and the nearest suitable airport
Aircraft ID, position, time, altitude, next fix and its estimated time
Equipment affected, the time it failed and when you last checked the VOR
final_quiz.why: 14 CFR 91.187(b) lists aircraft ID, equipment affected, degree of impairment of IFR capability, and nature and extent of assistance desired [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. The first list is a position report [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2d]].

final_quiz.q: You must cross a fix at 3,000 ft. You are at 9,000 ft, plan 500 fpm down, and expect a 120 knot groundspeed. How far before the fix should you start down?
options: 12 NM
24 NM
18 NM
36 NM
final_quiz.why: 6,000 ft ÷ 500 fpm = 12 minutes. 120 knots = 2 NM per minute, so 24 NM. Plan the descent so you reach the crossing altitude on time, as in the IPH descent planning task [[29:120|IPH 3-8]]. 12 NM confuses minutes with miles.

final_quiz.q: ATC says "Descend via the Eagul Five arrival, except after Geeno, maintain one zero thousand." What do you do after Geeno?
options: Level at 10,000 until ATC clears you lower
Climb back to the published altitude at Geeno
Descend to the STAR's bottom altitude at pilot's discretion
Continue descending via the remaining published altitudes
final_quiz.why: Fly the STAR's restrictions to Geeno, then maintain 10,000 until cleared by ATC to continue down [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]].

final_quiz.q: In IMC, your TIS-B display shows a target converging at your altitude. ATC hasn't said anything. What is right?
options: Turn away now on your own, since that is what the traffic display is for
Tell ATC and get approval first, unless it's an imminent emergency
Climb 500 ft on your own; small deviations in IMC don't need approval
Ignore it completely, because TIS-B targets are always false or stale
final_quiz.why: TIS-B is for awareness only, not collision avoidance. Except in an imminent emergency, deviations for TIS-B traffic need ATC approval first, because aircraft you can't see on the display may be nearby [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8d]].

final_quiz.q: Your FIS-B radar image is stamped 4 minutes old and shows a gap in a line of storms ahead. How should you use it?
options: Fly through the gap, because a 4 minute old image is current enough
Use it only after the storms have visibly moved past the gap
Trust it over ATC reports, since it updates every minute
Use it only for broad avoidance; it may be much older
final_quiz.why: Datalinked mosaics show where precipitation was and may be 15 to 20 minutes older than the indicated age [[28:327|AWH 24-43]]. NEXRAD is for strategic avoidance, never for navigating through storms [[28:25|AWH 3-2]].

final_quiz.q: In the CARBON VOR box on the excerpt, what MCA is printed for V134?
options: 8,100 ft westbound
10,200 ft westbound
10,200 ft eastbound
13,000 ft westbound
final_quiz.why: The box reads MCA V134 10200 W [[29:90|IPH Figure 2-49]].

final_quiz.q: How many airway and direction lines are in the yellow MCA box at JACKSON?
options: Three
One
Four
Two
final_quiz.why: It lists V520 14600 W and V330 13200 W [[29:97|IPH Figure 2-59]].

final_quiz.q: On the PENNS TWO ARRIVAL, what is the distance from HAYED to PENNS through RACKI?
options: 35 NM
23 NM
58 NM
45 NM
final_quiz.why: HAYED to RACKI is 22 NM and RACKI to PENNS is 23 NM, so 45 NM [[29:132|IPH Figure 3-17]].

final_quiz.q: You are on an airway in controlled airspace under IFR. Where must you fly?
options: Along the centerline of the airway
On the edge to stay clear of traffic
Within 4 NM either side of the airway
Anywhere inside the primary area
final_quiz.why: On an ATS route you fly along the centerline unless ATC authorizes otherwise [[60:482|14 CFR 91.181(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Under radar control, which position reports do you need to make?
options: Every designated compulsory reporting point
Only the fixes on the filed route
Only points ATC specifically requests
Only the first point after departure
final_quiz.why: While under radar control, only the reporting points ATC specifically requests need be reported [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183(a)]].
